newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Weathered Yeltsin launches another comeback.
newsitem.headline: Weathered Yeltsin launches another comeback.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin clocked up another political comeback on Monday when he returned to his Kremlin desk after months of illness and heart surgery, anxious to dispel doubts about his grasp on power.
After months of inactivity the strong-willed Russian leader clearly wants to reassert his grip quickly and decisively. But doctors say he should take things easy in order not to overstrain his heart.

"He will be torn between striving for power and seeking not to complicate his own life," political analyst Viktor Kuvaldin told NTV television on Sunday. "The man has been between life and death and we do not know what he is like after this."
Yeltsin, always at his best in a crisis, does not have an immediate storm to handle, although Russia's political and economic problems have piled up during his absence.

Living standards have plunged for millions of ordinary people and the gap has widened between rich and poor. A peace deal in the rebel Caucasus region of Chechnya is holding, but only just, and the economy is mired in a prolonged slump.
Yeltsin, 65 and set for almost four more years in office, has yet to forge a role for himself in the new era, although he promised Russians on Monday things would get better next year.
Some experts say Yeltsin's best option would be to try and assume the role of supreme arbiter, leaving the day-to-day running of Russia to his closest lieutenants.
But Yeltsin, for whom striving for power is something of a passion, may find this a difficult role to play.

In an interview televised on Friday Yeltsin clearly tried to resurrect his image of a strong leader. He said Russia needed an active president, new ideas and courage and he promised an energetic return to work in the Kremlin.
Yeltsin, who looked much thinner than before his surgery, spoke in a firm and decisive voice.
But he did not seem to have a trademark spark in his eyes -- probably only natural for a 65-year-old who underwent a quintuple bypass operation just seven weeks ago.

Yeltsin has had a roller-coaster career as a Communist Party official who became leader of the first legal opposition in the Soviet Union and who then crushed the party and played a pivotal role in destroying the Soviet Union.
He launched Russia's first market reforms and, in what might be considered his gravest mistake, spilt the blood of thousands of his countrymen in the breakaway region of Chechnya.

Two mild heart attacks last year put him out of action for months. But Yeltsin pulled out all the stops before the first round of the presidential election to prove he had what it took for four more years in power.
He criss-crossed the vast Russian Federation, wooing the crowds with a carefully managed Western-style campaign.
Gone was the halting walk, the slurred speech and the puffy face which had stirred rumours that heavy drinking and a weak heart might be taking their toll on him.

But Yeltsin disappeared with heart problems when his goal of reelection was already in sight, and has appeared only briefly since. The heart operation, conducted on November 5, aimed to enable him to live a normal life.

Yeltsin, elected Russian president in 1991, hit the peak of his power, strength and popularity in August of that year when, climbing atop a tank, he defied a hardline coup against Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev.

But two years after personifying the fight for democracy on the tank outside the White House, his moral authority slipped when he sent tanks against the same parliament building to crush a bloody rebellion by parliamentary hardliners.
In late 1994 Yeltsin committed what he later acknowledged to be a blunder, sending troops to Chechnya to end its drive for independence. Tens of thousands of people died in the fighting.
He now says he is committed to maintaining a fragile peace settlement there. "This is the course of the president, the course of the country," he said on Friday.
